data.name: Ironclads: American Civil War
data.detailed_description:
<p>Battle of the civil war ironclads. Take part in battles from USS Monitor vs CSS Virginia before battles between armored squadrons of steamships and other vessels.</p>
<p>The flow of time is organized into rounds. Within the limits of each round, the player and the computer opponent take turns executing all actions possible within five minutes of real time combat for each of their ships. At the moment when the selected active ship is carrying out an action, all other game units are motionless. Time for decision-making is not limited.</p>
<p>Game locations are presented in real 1:1 scale and are not divided into cells or hexagons. The trajectory of movement of the active ship is determined by laws of physics and calculated using realistic speed, size and shape of a unit.</p>
<p>The campaign based on alternate outcomes of events which assume a more favourable position for the Confederation in the first two years of the conflict, including diplomatic recognition and construction of a stronger, more balanced Southern fleet in European shipyards.</p>
<p>USA and CSA campaigns: 14 missions, 80 hours of game time, 54 unique ships. USS Monitor, CSS Virginia, USS New Ironsides and others Civil War ironclads 3d models.</p><br /><br />
<h2>Key features:</h2><ul>
<li>Historical accuracy: the game's locations are created based on historical maps and other surviving documents and accounts of real battles</li>
<li>3D models of the civil war ironclads and other warships are based on original drawings and designs from archives, or those restored by experts using photos, models and descriptions of the ships that participated in the Civil War</li>
<li>Realness: use of real specifications of the civil war ironclads and other warships: the size, hull contours, displacement, construction materials and design, quality and arrangement the crew and armament, speed and acceleration</li>
<li>Calculations of physical interactions such as collisions between ships, flooding and capsizing, shell modeling, ammunition fires and flooding</li>
<li>Use of a special ballistic calculator on the basis of original artillery tables for definition of accuracy, penetration ability, explosion and shrapnel damage</li>
</ul>

reviews.review:
Ironclads: American Civil War offers a distinctive approach to historical naval strategy by recreating the technological transformation of maritime combat during the American Civil War. Developed by Totem Games and published by Strategy First, the game focuses on the tactical challenges of commanding armored steam-powered warships rather than delivering conventional action-oriented naval battles. Its combination of historical vessels, calculated artillery exchanges, and deliberate maneuvering creates an experience designed primarily for enthusiasts of military history and detailed warfare simulations. Although its ambition is admirable, the game struggles with outdated presentation, slow combat progression, and accessibility issues that prevent its interesting concepts from reaching their full potential.

The gameplay revolves around commanding Union and Confederate vessels in tactical encounters where positioning, firepower, and defensive capabilities determine success. Famous ironclads such as the USS Monitor and CSS Virginia demonstrate the dramatic changes in shipbuilding technology that occurred during this period. Different vessels possess their own characteristics involving armor protection, artillery arrangements, speed, and maneuverability. These distinctions encourage players to evaluate their available ships carefully rather than treating every unit as interchangeable. The emphasis on historically inspired specifications adds authenticity, making individual engagements feel like exercises in naval command rather than straightforward exchanges of damage.

Combat follows an unusual turn-based structure in which individual ships perform actions while other vessels remain stationary. Each round represents approximately five minutes of simulated battle, allowing players to consider their decisions without time pressure. This approach encourages deliberate planning, particularly when coordinating firing positions and attempting to exploit an opponent's weaknesses. However, the system also creates an awkward rhythm. Naval warfare traditionally involves continuous movement and simultaneous actions, so watching vessels operate independently can undermine the illusion of a living battlefield. Larger engagements become especially tedious when numerous individual actions must be completed before the situation meaningfully changes.

One of the game's strongest elements is its dedication to technical simulation. Ship movements are influenced by physical properties rather than conventional grid-based navigation, with factors such as vessel dimensions, acceleration, and turning behavior affecting maneuverability. Damage modeling introduces additional complications, including flooding, structural deterioration, ammunition fires, and the possibility of capsizing. Artillery calculations consider historical ballistic behavior, accuracy, penetration, and explosive effects. These mechanics provide a satisfying degree of depth for players who appreciate understanding why a particular maneuver or attack succeeds. Unfortunately, the interface does not always communicate this complexity clearly, leaving certain outcomes feeling difficult to predict or interpret.

The campaign provides opportunities to command both sides of the conflict across 14 missions featuring a collection of 54 unique vessels. Its alternate-history elements introduce possibilities beyond strictly documented engagements, including scenarios involving a stronger Confederate naval presence. This creative direction gives the campaign additional variety while preserving its historical foundation. Rather than relying on elaborate storytelling, the game places most of its attention on battlefield decisions and the technical characteristics of the participating ships. This makes the experience particularly attractive to naval history enthusiasts, although players expecting cinematic narratives, memorable characters, or extensive strategic management outside combat may find the campaign relatively limited.

Visually, the game reveals its age through modest ship models, basic environments, restrained combat effects, and an interface that prioritizes functionality over convenience. The historical designs remain recognizable, and the vessels possess enough distinguishing characteristics to support the simulation's objectives. Nevertheless, battles lack the visual intensity that might make prolonged engagements more exciting. The presentation can also make important information harder to follow than necessary. Combined with the measured pace of combat, these limitations contribute to an experience that sometimes feels more like operating an older tactical simulation program than playing a polished modern strategy title.

The difficulty comes not simply from enemy opposition but from understanding how the various mechanics interact. Effective command requires patience, familiarity with ship capabilities, and a willingness to experiment with movement and firing positions. There is satisfaction in successfully positioning an armored vessel to withstand incoming attacks while delivering effective artillery fire. However, repetitive commands, limited feedback, and cumbersome controls can gradually reduce that satisfaction. Replayability depends largely on personal enthusiasm for historical naval engagements, since the core mechanics remain relatively consistent throughout the campaign.

Steam Deck compatibility remains unverified, with no confirmed official Steam Deck Verified or Playable classification. Although the game's modest hardware requirements suggest that processing power should not be a major obstacle, compatibility with SteamOS and Proton cannot be guaranteed. Its mouse-oriented controls and interface may also require customized input configurations, making handheld play potentially less comfortable than traditional desktop operation.

Ultimately, Ironclads: American Civil War is an ambitious but imperfect naval strategy game that prioritizes historical detail over accessibility and spectacle. Its realistic ship characteristics, artillery calculations, and distinctive tactical systems offer considerable appeal to dedicated simulation enthusiasts. However, sluggish combat, aging graphics, and unintuitive presentation make it difficult to recommend broadly. Players fascinated by nineteenth-century ironclad warfare may discover an intriguing historical experience beneath its rough exterior, while those seeking smooth controls and engaging action will likely find it frustrating.

A historically detailed and mechanically ambitious naval simulation that offers interesting tactical possibilities, but its cumbersome execution, dated presentation, and limited accessibility prevent it from becoming a truly compelling strategy experience.

Rating: 4/10
